13:
The passage gives two premises: severe penalties deter only if people think detection is fairly likely, and people think detection for drink-driving is very unlikely. Put together: severe penalties for drink-driving do not work as a deterrent — A.
B, D and E go beyond the passage; C assumes the perception is wrong, which the passage does not say.
1:
Crashes are most likely when the computer hands control back to a confused pilot. So removing that hand-over — fully automated, pilotless planes — would likely be safer than the current mix — A.
B and C are too strong; D and E are not discussed.
2:
The argument admits innocent people have been hanged but still says capital punishment ensures 'real justice'. That assumes real justice is possible despite occasional miscarriages — B.
A is too strong (the passage only says mistakes have 'receded').
3: You should confess because your micro-expressions will give you away. That only works if the other person can recognise those micro-expressions — B.
4: The audits measured only RFR, yet the argument concludes masts are safe 'and can be sited anywhere'. That assumes RFR is the only health risk from masts — E.
5:
The argument pushes washable nappies because disposables fill scarce landfill. C strengthens it: disposables take over 500 years to break down, so landfill keeps filling.
A and B weaken; D and E don't add support.
6: The argument: oppose the clubs because they risk wiping out endangered bears. C weakens it: bear numbers haven't really changed since the clubs began.
7: The argument says tits tear paper to look for food. A weakens it: they leave real food to tear paper, so food-seeking isn't the reason.
8:
Cows can't believe in a remedy, so the placebo effect can't explain their result. The trial shows the benefit in cows isn't a placebo effect — C.
A and B contradict the result; D and E go too far.
9: The argument praises 'ignoring logic and following common sense' as if they pull in opposite directions. That assumes logic and common sense can't both be followed — D.
10: The 'most important reason' against using hard shoulders is to keep Britain's good safety record. That assumes hard shoulders help create that record — E.
11: The palaeontologist argues T. rex was a scavenger and therefore not a predator. That assumes it couldn't have been both — C.
12:
Crime follows infant lead exposure with a 20-year lag, and Europe banned lead in the 1990s. So Europe could soon expect falling violent crime — A.
B, C and E are far too strong; D isn't supported.
14:
The 'Big Mac' generation's diet and habits put their health and life expectancy at risk. The sensible conclusion: they would be wise to change their lifestyle — D.
C and E go beyond the passage; A and B aren't supported.
15: Fewer pupils study languages, departments are closing, and languages matter for confidence abroad and international business. So British education doesn't prepare people well for a global world — A.
16: The argument says more alcohol explains rising crime by girls. B gives another explanation: girls are now more likely to be prosecuted, so recorded offences rose.
17:
The passage shows the same dishonest act can come from very different motives tied to personality. So one dishonest act doesn't mean a child will be dishonest in other situations — A.
B, C, D and E aren't supported.
18: Demand is rising faster than the donor-age population, shortages are appearing, and there is no substitute for blood. So the problem shows no sign of going away — E.
19: Legalising cannabis is meant to reduce use by making people aware of its dangers, as with tobacco. That assumes the dangers won't be widely known unless it is legal — B.
20: Falling graduate unemployment is taken to show the economy needs more graduates. That fails if graduates are simply taking jobs non-graduates used to do — so the argument assumes they are not — C.
21: The argument says big brains must be used for intelligence. C weakens it: large brains might be used for things other than intelligence.
22: The argument says subsidised farming in rich countries doesn't help the hungry, so the money should go to poor countries' agriculture. C supports this: much of the surplus rots before it can even be sent abroad.
